preserved_analysis.failure_mode_definition: A failure mode in which a governance corpus is amended, refactored, migrated, reorganised, or deterministically updated without a reliable higher-order review that checks cross-instrument doctrine freshness and preserves continuity-bearing instrument structures. The failure occurs when local edits remain readable or machine-valid but leave higher-order provisions stale, create cross-instrument contradiction or logic shear, or regenerate, compress, omit, rename, reorder, or otherwise transmute metadata, provenance, amendment history, canonical-code declarations, registry-facing fields, seals, or other structures necessary to identify and trace the instrument as the same constitutional object.
preserved_analysis.failure_threshold: The threshold is met where one or more requested governance changes are successfully applied at file or branch level, ordinary CI or local readability does not expose a blocking defect, and subsequent review finds that a higher-order or neighbouring instrument remained stale or contradictory; a source-authoritative standard was not propagated into constitutional or cross-domain doctrine; continuity-bearing metadata or provenance was approximated rather than preserved; canonical code, registry, schema, seal, or amendment-ledger structures were omitted or weakened; or the Human Governance Editor must reconstruct prior branch history and decision context to restore the corpus. A single cosmetic formatting difference is insufficient unless it materially affects lineage, authority, machine readability, reviewability, or instrument identity.

preserved_analysis.why_it_matters_to_CAM: CAM is a constitutional corpus rather than a collection of independent Markdown files. A change can pass ordinary CI, preserve valid references, and produce a readable local instrument while still weakening the corpus as a whole. If refactors approximate rather than copy forward provenance, canonical declarations, amendment history, source-authority fields, registry-facing metadata, and seal identity, the instrument loses constitutional traceability even when its topic and some body doctrine remain recognisable. If metadata or schema decisions are implemented without checking higher-order doctrine, the Constitution itself may become stale relative to the standards it is supposed to govern. This threatens source authority, custodial control, auditability, doctrinal coherence, reproducibility, and safe model-assisted governance maintenance.
